name: Opportunity Cost
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: What Else Your Ten Million Dollars Could Have Been Doing
lesson.summary: Opportunity cost measures a quantum investment against the next-best alternative use of the same capital, and once compared to something as ordinary as an index fund, the bar it needs to clear gets much higher.
lesson.body:
Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up by choosing one option over another. It never appears on an invoice, which is exactly why it is the most-forgotten number in capital allocation decisions, but it is entirely real: every dollar committed to a quantum computing initiative is a dollar that cannot simultaneously fund a classical HPC upgrade, be returned to shareholders, sit in a diversified index fund, or back a different R&D bet with a better-understood payoff.

Here is a worked example. A company has $10,000,000 and two options. Option A: fund a quantum computing pilot expected to be worth $12,500,000 in four years. Option B: invest the same $10,000,000 in a diversified equity index fund, which has historically returned roughly 9 to 10 percent annually in nominal terms over long horizons, or around 6 to 7 percent after inflation, though any single four-year stretch varies considerably. Using a conservative 8 percent nominal annual return for this comparison, compounded over four years: $10,000,000 times 1.08 to the fourth power equals $13,604,890.

Comparing the two: the quantum pilot returns $12,500,000, while the passive index alternative returns an estimated $13,604,890. The opportunity cost of choosing the quantum pilot is $13,604,890 minus $12,500,000, or $1,104,890, meaning the company would have ended up about $1.1 million better off, in this simplified comparison, simply parking the money in an index fund and doing nothing else. This is precisely the comparison quantum computing pitch decks almost never include. They compare the investment to doing nothing, a $0 baseline, when the honest baseline is the best realistic alternative use of the same capital, which for most companies is a liquid, diversified investment with a long, well-understood track record.

This does not mean quantum computing investment is never justified on financial grounds alone. Sometimes strategic value genuinely is not captured by an index-fund comparison, a company that needs the technical capability itself rather than just a financial return, or one racing a competitor for first-mover position. But that "next best alternative" comparison should be made explicitly and with real numbers, not waved away with a phrase like "innovation requires investment," which is true of literally every investment decision a company could ever make and therefore justifies none of them in particular.

Opportunity cost completes the ROI question from earlier in this book. ROI asks whether an investment made money. Opportunity cost asks the sharper question: did it make more money than the next-best thing available for the same dollars. Quantum computing R&D, given its long timelines, high uncertainty, and the high risk-adjusted hurdle rate established two chapters ago, has to clear a genuinely high opportunity-cost bar, not merely a better-than-zero bar, to be a sound decision on its financial merits alone.
